analysis.one_liner: Exempts pension plans from Dodd-Frank rules requiring swap dealers to act in their best interests.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees in 2011 without ever reaching a floor vote, leaving Dodd-Frank's conflict-of-interest protections for pension plans in place.
analysis.plain_summary: Dodd-Frank requires banks and other dealers who sell swaps to pension plans to act in the plan's best interests, disclose conflicts, and recommend that the plan hire an independent advisor. This bill would strip pension plans of that 'special entity' protected status, declare that swap dealers owe no fiduciary duty to retirement plans, and let a dealer escape those duties entirely if the plan signs a paper saying it will rely on its own advisor instead. It also loosens the rules for who counts as an 'independent' advisor, accepting a 10% revenue tie to the dealer as independent.
analysis.who_benefits: Major banks and other swap dealers that sell swaps to pension funds. They would no longer be held to a best-interests standard when trading with retirement plans, could shed the 'advisor' duties by getting a written representation from the plan, and would face a weaker test for whether the plan's outside advisor is truly independent of the dealer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks that sell swaps to pension funds

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no person becomes a fiduciary to an employee benefit plan by acting as a swap dealer or major swap participant, removing ERISA's fiduciary standard from dealer dealings with pensions [S2][S3].

It removes employee benefit plans and funds they invest in from the Dodd-Frank definition of a protected 'special entity,' ending the heightened business-conduct standards dealers owe those plans [S2][S3].

A swap dealer would not be treated as an advisor to a pension plan if the plan signs a written statement that it will not rely on the dealer's recommendations and the dealer discloses that it is not acting in the plan's best interests [S2][S3].

The bill states that a dealer's duty to act in a special entity's best interests is not a fiduciary standard under federal or state law, and sets looser independence criteria for the plan's advisor, including allowing advisors who derive up to 10% of gross revenues from the dealer [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pension plan participants and beneficiaries, whose retirement funds would lose the requirement that dealers act in the plan's best interests and disclose that they are doing so; the plan trustees would bear the risk instead.

drawbacks.text: Supporters' stated goal was ensuring pension plans can use swaps to hedge risks; to the extent Dodd-Frank's special-entity rules made hedging slower or costlier for smaller plans, or pushed dealers away from them, that is a genuine cost the bill addressed [S3].

The bill's escape hatch depends on the plan signing away reliance on the dealer, which in practice could occur under pressure from a dealer it needs to trade with, and the 10% revenue test would allow advisors with real financial ties to a dealer to count as 'independent' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Pension plans already retained the ability to use swaps to hedge under Dodd-Frank; the special-entity rules changed the dealer's conduct, not the plan's access. The bill's main effect was to remove the dealers' duty of care and weaken the independence safeguards, shifting risk onto retirement savers. Whatever hedging-efficiency benefit sponsors pointed to could have been addressed without stripping the best-interests duty, so the cost to plan beneficiaries outweighed the stated benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, got one favorable subcommittee vote in Financial Services, was passed along to another subcommittee, and never came up in full committee or on the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Quico Canseco (R-TX) introduced the bill on September 23, 2011, together with Rep. Scott Garrett, and it was referred to the Agriculture, Education and the Workforce, and Financial Services Committees [S1][S3][S5].
In November 2011 the Financial Services Subcommittee on Capital Markets held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee on a 19-14 vote [S5].
On November 18, 2011 it was referred to the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never received a vote in any full House committee or on the House floor, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pension plan participants came out ahead: the Dodd-Frank protections requiring dealers to act in a pension plan's best interests remained in force, and the banks that sell swaps to pension funds failed to win the exemption they sought.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the subcommittee's 19-14 roll call forwarding the bill; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were Republicans, and no full-chamber vote ever occurred [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Swap dealers (major banks and broker-dealers in derivatives)
industries.note: The bill would free dealers from the Dodd-Frank requirement to act in a pension plan's best interests and let them escape advisor duties with a signed paper. Dealers profit from pricing and structuring swaps against plans that lack dealer-level expertise, so removing the duty of care shifts the cost to retirement savers.

Pension plans would lose their 'special entity' protected status, and their beneficiaries would bear the risk of conflicted dealer conduct. The plans' interests in this bill run directly alongside ordinary savers' interests.

industries.industry: Independent swap advisors (registered investment advisers, commodity trading advisers, municipal advisors)
industries.note: The bill builds a safe harbor making plans that retain registered advisers presumptively protected, steering more advisory work to these firms, though it also loosens the independence standard to permit advisers earning up to 10% of revenue from a dealer.
